title: Joshua 24:14–28
context: Joshua calls the people to fear and serve the LORD in sincerity and truth, to put away the gods their fathers served, and to choose that day whom they will serve, declaring that he and his house will serve the LORD. The people pledge loyalty, recalling the exodus; Joshua warns that they cannot serve a holy and jealous God lightly, they insist, and he makes them witnesses against themselves, makes a covenant at Shechem, writes the words in the book of the law, and sets up a stone as witness. Both traditions share the call to wholehearted covenant loyalty; they differ mainly on how the choice in 24:15 relates to God’s enabling grace.

verses.text: “Now therefore fear the LORD, and serve him in sincerity and in truth. Put away the gods which your fathers served beyond the River, in Egypt; and serve the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Fear the LORD, serve him in sincerity and truth, and put away the gods of beyond the River and Egypt. Arminian readers note that the call follows directly from the recital of grace: “Now therefore.”

The mention of Egypt’s gods suggests idolatry had followed Israel (cf. Ezek 20:7–8).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see grace preceding command.

Sincerity and truth describe wholehearted, undivided service. Putting away idols is the outward sign of an inward turning to God (cf. 1 Sam 7:3).

verses.text: If it seems evil to you to serve the LORD, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
If serving the LORD seems evil, choose today whom you will serve; Joshua and his house will serve the LORD. Arminian readers see a genuine choice set before the people, enabled by God’s prior grace shown in verses 2–13 (cf. Deut 30:19).

They hold that God’s grace makes a real response possible for all who hear, and that it can be refused.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see a real choice and real responsibility.

They hold that a heart which truly chooses the LORD has been made willing by God’s effectual grace (cf. John 6:44; Phil 2:13), so the call is the means by which God brings his people to choose him. Both traditions agree that Joshua’s household example and his call are sincere.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm that the choice is real, that the people are responsible, and that God’s prior grace (vv. 2–13) is the ground of the call. Arminian readers hold that God’s enabling, prevenient grace makes it possible for every hearer to choose the LORD, while leaving the choice open to refusal. Reformed readers hold that those who truly choose the LORD do so because God’s effectual grace has renewed their hearts, so the call is the means by which he brings them to choose.

verses.text: The people answered, “Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD, to serve other gods;
verses.arminianNotes:
The people answer, “Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD, to serve other gods.” Arminian readers take the response as sincere and freely given in answer to Joshua’s call.

Their words will be tested in the generations that follow, which shows that a good beginning must be carried through.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see an appropriate first response to the recital of God’s grace.

The dialogue that follows presses whether the people’s intentions are strong enough, and Reformed readers see in that pressure a reminder that human resolve needs God’s sustaining grace.

verses.text: for it is the LORD our God who brought us and our fathers up out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, and who did those great signs in our sight, and preserved us in all the way in which we went, and among all the peoples through the middle of whom we passed.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people give their reason: the LORD brought them out of Egypt, did great signs, and preserved them on the way. Arminian readers note that they echo Joshua’s recital and own it as their story.

Their pledge is grounded in what God has done, not in their own strength.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the people confessing God’s saving deeds, using the phrase “house of bondage” found in the preface to the Ten Commandments (Exod 20:2).

Right response flows from remembered grace, a point both traditions affirm.

verses.text: The LORD drove out from before us all the peoples, even the Amorites who lived in the land. Therefore we also will serve the LORD; for he is our God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD drove out the peoples, “Therefore we also will serve the LORD; for he is our God.” Arminian readers note the logical “therefore”: grace received calls for a chosen response.

The people make their choice publicly and together.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see service as the fitting response to grace already given.

The confession “he is our God” expresses covenant belonging. The people do not make the LORD their God by choosing; they acknowledge the God who has already acted for them.

verses.text: Joshua said to the people, “You can’t serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God. He will not forgive your disobedience nor your sins.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua answers, “You can’t serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God.” Arminian readers usually read this as a sobering warning not to make the commitment lightly or with divided hearts.

The line about not forgiving disobedience is read against God’s mercy elsewhere (Exod 34:6–7), and interpreters discuss its exact force.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers often see the statement as exposing the people’s inability to serve God by their own strength, as later history shows (cf. Deut 31:16–21).

Both traditions agree that it warns against shallow commitment and that God’s holiness and jealousy are real (Exod 20:5; 34:14).

verses.text: If you forsake the LORD, and serve foreign gods, then he will turn and do you evil, and consume you, after he has done you good.”
verses.arminianNotes:
If they forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, he will turn and harm them after doing them good. Arminian readers note that the warning treats falling away as a real possibility with real consequences.

Past blessing does not guarantee future blessing for a people who abandon God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s just judgment on covenant unfaithfulness, which the later history of Israel confirms.

The warning is addressed seriously to the covenant community, and both traditions treat it as a real warning rather than an empty threat.

verses.text: The people said to Joshua, “No, but we will serve the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The people insist, “No, but we will serve the LORD.” Arminian readers note their determined response even after Joshua’s warning.

The choice is affirmed a second time, now with the cost in view.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a resolute pledge made with the warning still ringing.

Whether it will endure is the question the next generations answer (Judg 2:10–13), which shows how much depends on God’s continuing grace.

verses.text: Joshua said to the people, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the LORD yourselves, to serve him.” They said, “We are witnesses.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua tells them they are witnesses against themselves that they have chosen the LORD, and they reply, “We are witnesses.” Arminian readers note the solemn accountability attached to their choice.

They cannot later claim they did not understand what they promised.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the people binding themselves publicly before God and each other.

Their own testimony will stand against them if they turn away. Public vows were a normal part of covenant renewal in Israel.

verses.text: “Now therefore put away the foreign gods which are among you, and incline your heart to the LORD, the God of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now therefore put away the foreign gods which are among you, and incline your heart to the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the people are called to an inward turning they are responsible to make.

The call implies that foreign gods were still present among them even after their pledge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Scripture uses the same language of God inclining hearts to himself (1 Kings 8:58; Ps 119:36).

Both traditions hold that the command is real and that God’s grace is necessary for the heart to turn. Putting away idols is the visible sign of that turning (cf. Gen 35:2–4).

verses.text: The people said to Joshua, “We will serve the LORD our God, and we will listen to his voice.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The people say, “We will serve the LORD our God, and we will listen to his voice.” Arminian readers note that this is their third affirmation, now adding a pledge to obey.

The repetition shows a commitment made with growing clarity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the covenant pledge complete in its essentials: service and listening.

Listening to God’s voice is the heart of covenant faithfulness, and the people’s promise sets the standard by which their later history is measured.

verses.text: So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and made for them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua makes a covenant with the people and sets a statute and an ordinance in Shechem. Arminian readers note the formal covenant renewal, like the one at Sinai (Exod 24:3–8).

Shechem becomes a place of covenant memory for Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the covenant renewed with a new generation through a human mediator.

The covenant is not new in substance. God’s existing covenant is reaffirmed and applied to the people now living in the land.

verses.text: Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God; and he took a great stone, and set it up there under the oak that was by the sanctuary of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua writes these words in the book of the law of God and sets up a great stone under the oak by the sanctuary of the LORD. Arminian readers note the written record, in line with Moses’ practice (Deut 31:24–26).

The oak near Shechem recalls Jacob’s burial of foreign gods there (Gen 35:4).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the covenant recorded in writing as part of God’s word to his people.

The stone serves as a lasting physical memorial alongside the written words. The precise relation of this “book of the law of God” to the books of Moses is not spelled out in the text.

verses.text: Joshua said to all the people, “Behold, this stone shall be a witness against us, for it has heard all the LORD’s words which he spoke to us. It shall be therefore a witness against you, lest you deny your God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua says the stone will be a witness because it has heard all the LORD’s words. Arminian readers note the vivid personification, similar to the witness heap in Genesis 31:44–48.

The stone is a reminder that their commitment was made openly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a memorial that will testify to the covenant if the people deny their God.

The stone stands as a silent witness, joining the people’s own testimony (v. 22) and the written record (v. 26).

verses.text: So Joshua sent the people away, each to his own inheritance.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua sends the people away, each to his own inheritance. Arminian readers note that the ceremony ends and covenant life must now be lived out in ordinary places.

Judges 2:6 picks up the story from this point.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the people returning home under covenant obligation.

Each tribe now lives out its promises in its own inheritance. The land God gave becomes the setting for daily faithfulness.
